newsitem.title: TAIWAN: MasterCard launches Taiwan secure system.
newsitem.headline: MasterCard launches Taiwan secure system.

text.p: MasterCard International in Taiwan on Friday launched a newly developed security protocol to guard against hackers trying to steal Internet transaction data.
The protocol -- Secure Electronic Transaction, or SET -- would be adopted by seven MasterCard members in Taiwan, enabling cardholders to enjoy security while making their purchases via the Internet.

Two leading card issuing banks -- China Trust Commercial and U.S. Citibank's Taiwan branch -- on Friday became the first financial institutions in the world to succeed in cross-bank transaction using the highly secured branded digital protocol, a MasterCard official said.
"Transaction through SET is almost 100 percent safe," Thomas Pouliet, MasterCard's vice president for electronic commerce, told Reuters in an interview.
"It would take a hacker at least a year to use four super computers to break into SET to get perhaps not even one complete credit card number," he said.
"It is therefore very, very safe to use SET to shop around via the Internet," Pouliot said.

SET was jointly developed by MasterCard and Visa International in association with a consortium of technology providers as a method to secure payment transactions over open networks, MasterCard officials said.
The SET protocol uses cryptography to provide confidentiality of information, ensure payment integrity and authenticate both merchants and cardholders.
Under the operation, cardholders would only need to click the MasterCard logo and the transaction would be automatically carried out.

A merchant can read from the information sent to it through SET only the items a cardholder wants to buy, and only the payment institution has all the necessary identification and security information of the cardholder.
"The introduction of SET will increase consumer and merchant confidence in on-line transactions using MasterCard," Pouliot said.
Because of its security, SET was expected to become the mainstream in future electronic transactions, he said.
He said MasterCard decided to choose Taiwan to launch the new system because the island is an important market where sophisticated technology is available.
The booming Taiwan market saw some 5.5 million credit card holders use their plastic to ring up a total of T$272.4 billion (US$9.9 billion) in 1996 -- up 40 percent from 1995.
MasterCard has one third of the market share in Taiwan.

"I believe electronic commerce is a high growth potential area. There are currently over 40 million Internet users in the world. Taiwan alone has some 800,000 accounts," said Charles Lo, executive vice president of ChinaTrust.
He said his bank will first choose 2,000 of its card members for testing between August and September before officially introducing the service in October.
MasterCard has 404 million credit and debit cards that are accepted at more than 1.3 million locations worldwide. In 1996, its gross dollar volume generated exceeded US$550 billion.

In Singapore, several thousand Visa cardholders from participating banks there are expected to use SET technology to make secure Internet purchases from a range of local suppliers from mid-1997. (US$1 = T$27.5)
